journal_name: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics

abstracts.abstract: We propose a novel compositional semantic framework grounded in perceptual simulation that fundamentally reconceptualizes how meaning arises in natural language processing. Departing from traditional distributional approaches that treat word vectors as primitive semantic atoms, our theory posits that lexical semantics emerges from embodied sensorimotor experience. We introduce the Perceptual Grounding Semantics (PGS) formalism, which models semantic composition through mental simulation processes analogous to human conceptualization. This paradigm shift enables formal treatment of metaphor, figurative language, and context-dependent interpretation as natural consequences of perceptual grounding rather than peripheral phenomena. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that PGS provides superior explanatory power for psycholinguistic phenomena including semantic priming effects and graded typicality judgments. We prove that semantic compositionality can be achieved through iterative perceptual simulation operators that preserve compositional structure while allowing context-sensitive interpretation. The framework generates testable predictions regarding processing difficulty that we validate through comprehension experiments. This work establishes that embodied semantic theories, traditionally considered too psychologically grounded for computational implementation, can provide rigorous formal foundations for next-generation language understanding systems, opening new research directions at the intersection of computational linguistics, cognitive science, and natural language processing.

We present a substantially refined formal theory of focus semantics that resolves critical limitations in existing information structure accounts within computational linguistics. While prior frameworks based on alternatives semantics or segmenting approaches have made significant contributions, they struggle to capture the full range of focus-sensitive operators across languages with flexible word order. Our Enhanced Focus Projection Theory (EFPT) introduces hierarchically structured focus domains that dynamically propagate semantic values through syntactic trees using constrained type-shifting operations. This refined formalization enables precise compositional treatment of focus particles, prosodic phrasing, and question-answer congruence that existing accounts handle only partially. We prove EFPT's correctness through compositionality theorems and demonstrate its explanatory superiority on a typologically diverse corpus of focus constructions. The theory's formal apparatus extends traditional type-driven semantics with novel semantic features capturing discourse coherence relations that trigger focus interpretation. Cross-linguistic validation on Mandarin, Hungarian, and Bantu data confirms EFPT's predictive coverage exceeds alternatives by 23% on held-out phenomena. Our analysis reveals that focus projection is fundamentally constrained by information structure principles rather than syntactic configuration alone, contributing to ongoing debates in formal semantics regarding the interface between syntax and discourse pragmatics. This work demonstrates that careful formal refinement of established theories can yield substantial theoretical and empirical advances in modeling natural language interpretation.

We introduce NeuroSymbolic Language Understanding (NSLU), a novel architecture that fundamentally reconceptualizes language understanding by tightly integrating symbolic logical reasoning with neural representation learning. Unlike conventional end-to-end neural approaches that treat reasoning as emergent behavior, NSLU explicitly separates declarative knowledge representation from inferential processing while maintaining full differentiable training. The symbolic component encodes linguistic knowledge as interpretable logical forms that support explicit inference chains, while the neural component handles fuzzy pattern recognition and generalization. We design a novel interface mechanism called Semantic Binding Networks that dynamically maps between symbolic representations and continuous embeddings without information loss, enabling the system to leverage both symbolic precision and neural flexibility. NSLU's architecture supports multi-hop reasoning through explicit symbolic chaining while retaining the ability to learn from raw text through neural encoding modules. Extensive evaluation across question answering, textual entailment, and logical deduction tasks demonstrates that NSLU achieves unprecedented performance on compositional generalization benchmarks that require systematic reasoning, while maintaining interpretable reasoning traces. The system produces explicit proof structures that can be inspected and verified, addressing the transparency challenges that have limited adoption of neural approaches in high-stakes applications. This paradigm represents a fundamental departure from the pure neural paradigm, demonstrating that neurosymbolic integration enables capabilities neither component achieves alone.

We present a substantially improved dialogue system architecture that significantly advances state-of-the-art performance in multi-turn conversation through novel mechanisms for discourse modeling and response generation. Existing dialogue systems suffer from consistency failures and shallow discourse modeling, often treating each turn in isolation. Our Multi-Resolution Discourse Transformer (MRDT) introduces hierarchical discourse representations that capture conversation structure at utterance, turn, and session levels simultaneously. The core innovation lies in a novel Disentangled Discourse Attention mechanism that separately models topical progression, sentiment evolution, and user intent trajectories, enabling more coherent long-term conversation. We design a Constrained Response Decoding strategy that guarantees logical consistency with prior dialogue states while maintaining response diversity. Training employs a multi-task objective combining next-utterance prediction with discourse coherence metrics, substantially improving performance on long conversations requiring reference maintenance. Evaluation on the Multi-Session Dialogue dataset demonstrates that MRDT achieves a 31% improvement in conversational coherence ratings and 18% improvement in user satisfaction over previous best systems. Ablation studies confirm that each architectural component contributes independently to overall performance gains. The system produces interpretable discourse state representations that enable targeted error analysis and controlled generation. This work demonstrates that sophisticated discourse modeling, when properly integrated into neural dialogue architectures, yields substantial practical improvements in conversation quality, advancing the state of the art in dialogue systems research.
